slides.title: Should Parcelbird launch its own quick-commerce grocery delivery service in 2027?

paragraphs.text: Should Parcelbird launch its own quick-commerce grocery delivery service in 2027?
Assessment of the Parcelbird Now proposal and recommendation to the board · Board meeting, January 2027
Parcelbird
Board (two founders and two investors)
Prepared from the board briefing pack only (synthetic benchmark data); no external research

slides.title: Executive summary

paragraphs.text: Executive summary
Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; invest in the software business, which can reach profitability within current cash
The market is growing fast, but no operator makes money in it
–	The launch case needs six conditions to hold, and the evidence supports none of them
–	GMV grew 42% a year in 2022–25, yet both incumbents lose money on every order and one is retreating
A dark store would lose money on every order, and customers leave before repaying their acquisition cost
–	It loses $6.17 per order at the median and $1.76 at best observed; only a plan beyond any real site profits
–	Our pop-up lost $12.57 per order, and only 22% of its customers were still ordering in month 3
Even on the founders' own numbers, the launch breaks the investors' cash constraints
–	It needs $9.5M against $7.2M spendable above the runway floor; with core burn, cash runs out in month 13
The software business is a better use of the same cash
–	It breaks even in about month 26 at 60% growth and keeps 12 months of runway while growth stays at 34%+
Decline the launch, back the software plan with phased hires, and set triggers before any re-entry
–	Approve $0.8M a year of hires in tranches, build a store-based offer for grocers, track four triggers

slides.title: We started from the founders' answer, "launch", and tested the six conditions it needs; the evidence supports none of them

paragraphs.text: We started from the founders' answer, "launch", and tested the six conditions it needs; the evidence supports none of them
Initial hypothesis tested: “Parcelbird should launch Parcelbird Now: 9 dark stores in 3 cities, contribution-positive per order by month 18”

data: 1. A profit pool exists, not just growth
GMV +42% a year, but −$1.90 (Zipcart) and −$3.40 (QuickBasket) per order; QuickBasket shut 36% of its cities
2. A store makes money at achievable inputs
−$6.17 per order at benchmark median; −$1.76 even with every best-observed input combined
3. We run stores better than the benchmark
The pop-up was below the median on all four drivers: AOV, promotions, riders, density
4. Customers stay long enough to repay their cost
$38 acquisition cost; 22% still ordering in month 3; never repaid at benchmark or pop-up economics
5. The plan fits cash with 12 months of runway
$9.5M needed against $7.2M spendable above the runway floor; no new funding expected
6. It beats the best other use of the cash
The software business breaks even within current cash if ARR growth stays at 34% or more

paragraphs.text: The hypothesis fails on every condition, so we reverse it

slides.title: Quick commerce is growing 42% a year, but both incumbents lose money on every order and one is already retreating

US quick-commerce grocery GMV, $ billions, 2022–25
None of that growth has become profit
GMV growth a year, 2022–25
▪	Zipcart: −26% EBITDA margin (−$310M on $1,200M), −$1.90 an order; positive only in its densest city, after a fee rise
▪	QuickBasket: −46% margin (−$96M on $210M), −$3.40 an order; closed 4 of its 11 cities (36%)
Growth alone does not justify entry: "nobody owns the Midwest" may simply mean nobody has made it pay

slides.title: Only the founders' plan makes money; even the best-observed result on every driver at once loses $1.76 per order

paragraphs.text: 1 Market    2 Economics    3 Funding    4 Alternative    5 Decision
Only the founders' plan makes money; even the best-observed result on every driver at once loses $1.76 per order
Contribution per order by input scenario, $ per order, before and after site fixed cost
No combination of observed inputs makes money
▪	Best observed: the best AOV ($42) and the best density (1,400 orders a day) come from different sites; combining them is already optimistic, and it still loses money
▪	Nine stores: −$2.0M a store a year means −$18.2M for the median network and −$8.1M at best observed; only the plan's inputs give a profit, +$11.9M
▪	Break-even AOV: with other inputs held, the median store needs $63 and the best-observed store $50, against a median of $34 and a best of $42
1  Inputs (AOV, promotions, orders per rider-hour, orders a day): pop-up $31, 12%, 2.1, 280; median $34, 6%, 2.4, 900; best $42, 6%, 3.0, 1,400; plan $45, 2%, 3.5, 1,800
2  After site fixed cost spreads each store's $1.15M a year of rent, staff and utilities (pop-up $0.65M); both measures exclude HQ overhead, capex and marketing
Sources: Parcelbird board briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis

slides.title: The plan must beat the best site observed on all four drivers; median AOV or rider productivity alone turns it loss-making

paragraphs.text: 1 Market    2 Economics    3 Funding    4 Alternative    5 Decision
The plan must beat the best site observed on all four drivers; median AOV or rider productivity alone turns it loss-making
Plan contribution per order after site fixed cost, with one driver at the benchmark median, $ per order
The plan needs more than the best site on every driver
▪	AOV: $45, 7% above the best site's $42 (median $34); promotions: 2% of AOV, 4 percentage points below the best site's 6%
▪	Riders and density: 3.5 orders per rider-hour and 1,800 orders a day, 17% and 29% above the top of the observed ranges (1.9–3.0 and 400–1,400)
▪	Exposure: at the median, AOV or rider productivity alone turns the plan negative; density or promotions alone leave a thin $0.2–0.3 per order, with nothing for HQ overhead or marketing
Scale check: nine plan stores would sell $266M a year, more than QuickBasket's $210M revenue
1  9 stores × 1,800 orders a day × $45 × 365 = $266M, about 5% of the 2025 US market; GMV taken as roughly equal to an operator's revenue
Sources: Parcelbird board briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis

paragraphs.text: The pop-up is our only test of a capability edge
▪	The claim: "we know how to run them better than anyone"; the pop-up did worse than the median of the stores our software runs
▪	Against the median: AOV 9% lower, promotions twice as high, 13% fewer orders per rider-hour, 69% fewer orders a day
▪	Fair caveat, it was early: orders grew 18% a week, from about 178 a day to about 407 in week 6 (our estimate), but with 12% promotions and $38 CAC
Ramp-up alone does not close the gap: even at median density the store would still lose $6.17 per order (p. 5)
